title: Her father's illness
hookLine: a childhood vision of a man with his face covered makes sense years later, when her father falls ill
tomorrow: how do you love the one person who grates on you most?

lines: NEWS SAID IN A LOW VOICE.
cards: Some family news only gets said in the car, or in a low voice in the kitchen: an uncle who's not himself lately, a parent in the hospital for something nobody names. Thérèse carried a strange memory like that.

As a small girl, at a window, she saw a man walking in the garden, dressed like her father, his height, his walk, but stooped, and with his head covered by a kind of apron. Her father was away from home.
She called out to him. The man walked on and was gone. Her sisters told her not to think about it.
So why did she see a covered face?

teach.b: She found her answer years later, inside Carmel. Not long after she entered, her father, Louis Martin, the man she called her king, fell ill in his mind.
He had to be cared for in a hospital, away from home, among strangers. People talked. She doesn't hide any of it in The Story of a Soul; she calls it a humiliation, for him and for the whole family.
Looking back, she reads the garden as a sign: her father's face, covered, the way Christ's face was hidden in his Passion. Here's the piece that solves the puzzle.
Her full name in Carmel was Thérèse of the Child Jesus and of the Holy Face.

That devotion leans on Isaiah's servant of God, in the Douay-Rheims: "Despised, and the most abject of men, a man of sorrows, and acquainted with infirmity." The prophet adds that even his look was hidden.

So Thérèse learned to look for Christ in a face nobody wanted to look at, starting with her own father's. One more thing to tell a friend tonight: she writes that she wouldn't trade those painful years for any ecstasy.
She doesn't say they were easy. She says love grew right where it hurt.

how: Catholics pray for the sick, including those with mental illness, at Mass and in private prayer, and devotion to the Holy Face meditates on Christ's suffering face in his Passion.

games.q: at a family party, your cousins start joking about an uncle who's been in the hospital for depression. what does Thérèse's holy face point you toward?
o: don't join the joke; keep seeing him with the same love as before.
laugh along once, so the party doesn't turn awkward for everyone.
agree that nobody should mention him again until he's well.
games.why: Thérèse looked for Christ's face in her father's, at his most humiliated. The illness didn't make him less her king, and it didn't make him a joke.

practice: Find a photo of someone in your family, on your phone or on a shelf, and look at the face slowly, the way Thérèse learned to look at a face others turned from.
While the sit runs, hold in mind the families living with mental illness, the ones who say it out loud and the ones who can only whisper it.
If anyone you know is in danger right now, call 988 in the US, or your local emergency number.
